newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Chaos at Belgian ports as French strike goes on.
newsitem.headline: Chaos at Belgian ports as French strike goes on.

text.p: Lorries forced to detour through Belgium by the French road hauliers' strike clogged the country's ports on Thursday, with massive queues developing and lengthy waiting times to board ferries bound for Britain.
The strike was also beginning to hit Belgian industry with manufacturers forced to devise costly alternative supply routes.

At Ostend a spokesman for Stena-Sally Lines reported sailings to Ramsgate fully booked for freight, with drivers having to wait in line for up to 10 hours to get on board. The spokesman said they were being given free coffee and sandwiches.

The company normally runs sailings between the English port of Dover and Calais in France, but as a result of the French truckers' blockade of Calais ships had been diverted to the Flemish port of Zeebrugge.
The Zeebrugge-Dover crossing takes three times as long, adding to the tailbacks on the Belgian side.

At Zeebrugge a spokesman for the port gendarmerie said queues of more than 1,000 trucks that built up on Wednesday had if anything got longer, with drivers having to wait up to 20 hours to get aboard sailings to Dover.
Tailbacks stretched back eight kilometres (five miles) on access roads, while there was a five kilometre (three mile) queue in the port.
Roadside restaurants and shops were doing a brisk trade.
A spokesman for P&O ferries said seven ferry loads of trucks were waiting to board its ships. "That is four times as many lorries as otherwise at this time of year."
The company said it had laid on five freight ferries, against the two which usually sail from Zeebrugge.
"With the blockade of Calais and the closure of the Channel Tunnel it is doubly busy here," the spokesman said.
The tunnel has been closed since November 18 when a truck fire gutted a section.
A Belgian Transport Association spokesman said the French strike, now in its 11th day, was costing Belgian haulage firms millions of francs.
Trucks could not get to Spain by road at all. Getting to Italy involved detouring through Luxembourg, Germany and Switzerland which has a 28-tonne weight limit, he said.

The De Standaard newspaper reported on Wednesday that the Belgian plant of French car maker Renault had been forced to shut its doors temporarily because supplies of parts for assembly were stranded in France.

A spokesman for Volvo Belgium said on Thursday the company had asked haulage firms to use alternative routes to ensure parts could reach its plant. "Parts are getting to us later and irregularly," he said.
